Russian Literature. Particularly of the nineteenth century, Russian literature represents one of the world's supreme literary traditions—a body of works of unmatched psychological depth, philosophical seriousness, and formal innovation. Emerging in the shadow of European Romanticism yet developing distinctly Russian preoccupations, Russian literature achieved its apotheosis in the novels of Fyodor Dostoevsky, Leo Tolstoy, and Ivan Turgenev.

Nineteenth-century Russia was an empire in crisis. Serfdom was abolished in eighteen sixty-one. Rapid industrialization and social upheaval followed. There was ideological ferment between Slavophiles and Westerners, nihilists, socialists, and anarchists. Russian literature inherited European Romanticism but developed distinctive concerns with the Russian soul, the suffering Christ, redemption, and the intellectual's moral burden. The novel became a philosophical form—Russian writers treated it as a vehicle for exploring ultimate questions of belief, meaning, and morality. Plot was secondary to spiritual and ethical inquiry.

Leo Tolstoy lived from eighteen twenty-eight to nineteen ten. His masterpieces War and Peace and Anna Karenina, published in eighteen sixty-nine and eighteen seventy-seven respectively, are epic novels of vast scope. They interweave personal, historical, and philosophical narratives. Characters wrestle with love, death, faith, and the meaning of history. Fyodor Dostoevsky, who lived from eighteen twenty-one to eighteen eighty-one, brought unprecedented psychological complexity to the novel. Crime and Punishment explores the interior life of a murderer with terrifying honesty, treating the crime as a spiritual crisis rather than merely a legal transgression. The Idiot, Demons, and The Brothers Karamazov followed. These works display psychological intensity and explore nihilism, faith, suffering, and redemption through Christ figures and moral transgression.

Ivan Turgenev lived from eighteen eighteen to eighteen eighty-three. He developed a more lyrical, contemplative realism, emphasizing interiority and the unresolved tensions within consciousness. His novel Fathers and Sons, published in eighteen sixty-two, introduced the nihilist archetype through the character Bazarov and explored generational conflict. Anton Chekhov lived from eighteen sixty to nineteen four. He refined Russian realism into concentrated form through short stories and plays. His masterpieces include The Cherry Orchard and Uncle Vanya. His work emphasizes psychological realism, emotional restraint, and the insignificance of individual lives in the vast cosmos.

Russian literature is distinguished by psychological depth—the exploration of consciousness with intensity rarely matched. Characters' inner lives are the primary narrative material. Philosophical seriousness is everywhere. Novels grapple with metaphysical questions—the existence of God, suffering, nihilism, redemption—as narrative imperatives. The Russian Christ is a recurrent figure—the innocent sufferer or redemptive victim. Dostoevsky in particular drew on Christianity as a source of meaning. Realism combines with intensity—detailed, realistic depiction of social life combined with heightened moral and emotional stakes. Russian writers also pioneered formal innovation, experimenting with narrative structure, point of view, and the relationship between narration and character, anticipating modernism itself.

Central to Russian preoccupation was the tension between nihilism and faith—the tension between scientific materialism and spiritual hunger. Belief in God becomes a form of rebellion and affirmation. Suffering is treated as redemptive—pain and trauma as paths to spiritual transformation and compassion. The suffering innocent redeems the guilty. The burden of consciousness weighs heavily—intelligence and self-awareness become sources of paralysis and anguish. The intellectual is trapped between action and doubt. And there runs throughout a preoccupation with Russian destiny and spiritual uniqueness, an oscillation between Westernization and native Slavic identity.

Russian literature shaped modernism profoundly. T. S. Eliot, James Joyce, Virginia Woolf engaged deeply with Russian novels. Dostoevsky in particular prefigures Freudian psychology through the exploration of repressed desire and neurosis. The philosophical novel becomes canonical—questions of meaning and morality are legitimate literary concerns. Twentieth-century figures like Thomas Mann, Hermann Hesse, and Rainer Maria Rilke all engage with Russian examples.
